podcast.body: This song appears on The Clash's album London Calling. It is a cover of an original song by American singer Vince Taylor, released in April 1959. "The clash and brand new Cadillac from the London Calling album. That's a cover by the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was recorded for the *London Calling* album, serving as a warm-up track on the first day in the studio with producer Guy Stevens. Stevens, prioritizing feel over technical perfection, rolled the tape machines as the band warmed up. Despite The Clash's confusion and belief that the take was "all wrong" due to tempo changes, Stevens insisted on using it, famously stating, "all rock and roll speeds up." The recording captures a live-off-the-floor energy with no overdubs or second chances.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song, featured on the "London Calling" album, serves as an example of The Clash's raw, uncorrected recording style from 1979. The band's tendency to play faster and faster as the song progressed, a natural imperfection, adds energy and was embraced by producer Guy Stevens, who stated, "all rock and roll speeds up." Such an organic tempo change would likely be "fixed" in modern production using tools like Pro Tools. "Did you notice how the band kept playing faster and faster throughout the song?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song, originally by Vince Taylor, was the first track The Clash worked on for their "London Calling" album. Producer Guy Stevens secretly recorded their warm-up, declaring it a "take" despite the band's protests about sloppiness and tempo issues. Stevens' rationale was, "hey, all rock and roll speeds up," establishing the raw recording approach for the entire album. "And the first song they decided to work on was called brand new Cadillac."
